Lesson 269.1 - VPC, Subnet, CIDR, Internet Gateway, NACL and Network Gateway

Design an isolated AWS network: address space, subnets, routes, gateways, and firewall layers.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

This lesson is a deep dive into designing an isolated AWS network: dividing its address space, controlling routes, filtering traffic, connecting private resources, and diagnosing communication failures.

  • Tab 1 covers what a VPC is: the problem it solves, logical isolation, and the default VPC versus a custom VPC, with worked diagrams of both.
  • Tab 2 covers the AWS VPC components: the five core components and the five connectivity components, and which lesson covers each one.
  • Tab 3 covers how Amazon VPC works end to end, following the official AWS documentation: VPCs and subnets, route tables, internet access paths, corporate network access, connecting VPCs, and the AWS private global network.
  • Tab 4 covers CIDR blocks and IP addressing: the 2^(32 − prefix) formula, reserved addresses, and the rules for choosing ranges.
  • Tab 5 covers subnets and route tables: how a VPC is partitioned into subnets, subnet sizing, how route tables give each subnet its behavior, public versus private subnets, and why multi-AZ matters.
  • Tab 6 covers the Internet Gateway: its key properties, how it defines public and private subnets, how it translates addresses, the steps to enable internet access, and how it compares with NAT gateways and egress-only Internet Gateways, with a hands-on lab.
  • Tab 7 covers the egress-only Internet Gateway: outbound-only IPv6 internet access, how it differs from a NAT gateway and an Internet Gateway, and what else changes in a dual-stack VPC.
  • Tab 8 covers security groups and network ACLs: stateful instance-level security groups, stateless subnet-level network ACLs, rule evaluation, ephemeral ports, and when to use each, with hands-on labs and an exam-style question.
  • Tab 9 is a hands-on demonstration of creating your first custom VPC in the AWS console, following the AWS Networking Workshop.
  • Tab 10 checks your understanding with open-ended questions.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Define a VPC and list the properties of the default VPC versus a custom VPC.
  2. Identify the five core VPC components and the five connectivity components (VPC peering, Transit Gateway, VPC endpoints, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect) and state each one’s purpose in one sentence.
  3. Explain how Amazon VPC works end to end: how subnets, route tables, and gateways combine to control where traffic can go.
  4. Explain how route tables control subnet traffic: the local route, main versus custom route tables, subnet associations, and route targets.
  5. Explain when to use an egress-only Internet Gateway for outbound-only IPv6 traffic, and how it differs from a NAT Gateway and an Internet Gateway.
  6. Calculate total and usable IP addresses for any CIDR block using the 2^(32 − prefix) formula and the five reserved addresses per subnet.
  7. Size a subnet for a required number of instances, accounting for the five reserved addresses.
  8. Configure internet access for a custom VPC using an Internet Gateway, and troubleshoot an instance that cannot reach the internet.
  9. Differentiate public from private subnets by their routing, and explain why a subnet is bound to exactly one Availability Zone.
  10. Differentiate security groups from network ACLs, and design a security group chain and NACL rule set for a three-tier application.
  11. Justify CIDR planning decisions (range choice, non-overlap, sizing) for environments that will grow and interconnect.

1. What Is a VPC?

Problem Statement

Imagine AWS without VPCs: one flat, shared network where every customer’s resources sit side by side, and anything could potentially talk to anything. Your database would share a network segment with a stranger’s web scraper. No company could run regulated workloads that way. The questions every organization asks:

  • How do we get our own private section of the AWS cloud, invisible to every other customer?
  • How do we control the IP ranges, subnets, and routing ourselves, the way our network team always has?
  • How do we keep workloads isolated by default, opening only the paths we deliberately choose?

Amazon VPC is the answer: a logically isolated virtual network per customer, with you in full control.

1.1 Definition and Isolation Guarantees

An Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own logically isolated virtual network within the AWS cloud. You control the virtual networking environment completely: the IP address range, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Properties to know precisely:

  • Regional scope — a VPC spans all Availability Zones in one Region, never across Regions.
  • Complete isolation — from other AWS customers, and from your own other VPCs: even two VPCs in the same account have no default connectivity between them. Nothing crosses a VPC boundary until you build the path (peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink — see the connectivity topic pages).
  • Quota — up to 5 VPCs per Region by default; a soft limit raisable via a quota increase request.
  • Nearly everything you launch — EC2, RDS, load balancers, ECS tasks, VPC-attached Lambda — lives inside a VPC subnet.

1.1.1 What a VPC Does: Three Core Capabilities

An Amazon VPC is primarily focused on the following capabilities:

What a VPC Does: Three Core Capabilities.
CapabilityWhat it meansMain tools
IsolationIsolating your own AWS resources from other AWS accounts.The VPC boundary itself, with your own private IP range
ProtectionProtecting your AWS resources deployed in the VPC from network threats.Security groups, network ACLs, private subnets
RoutingRouting network traffic to and from your resources deployed in the VPC.Route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, endpoints, VPN

Every component you will study in this series serves one of these three jobs. When an exam question describes a requirement, ask which job it is: keep it apart (isolation), keep threats out (protection), or get traffic where it needs to go (routing).

1.1.2 An Example VPC

The following diagram shows an example VPC. The VPC has one subnet in each of the Availability Zones in the Region, EC2 instances in each subnet, and an internet gateway to allow communication between the resources in your VPC and the internet.

1.2 Default VPC vs. Custom VPC

Every Region in your account comes with a default VPC, pre-configured and ready to use. For anything that matters, you create a custom VPC and make every decision deliberately:

Default VPC vs. Custom VPC.
AspectDefault VPCCustom VPC
Created byAWS — one per Region, automaticallyYou, deliberately
CIDRAlways 172.31.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses)You choose, between /16 and /28
SubnetsOne public subnet pre-created in every AZ (/20 each)Blank — you design them
Internet GatewayAttached, with the 0.0.0.0/0 route already in the main route tableYou create, attach, and route explicitly
DNS hostnamesEnabled — instances with public IPs get public DNS namesDisabled until you enable it
Best forQuick tests, learning, proofs of conceptEvery production workload

Walk the diagram: the EC2 instance in subnet 1 holds private IP 172.31.0.5 for traffic inside the VPC and public IP 203.0.113.17 for the internet. Its subnet (172.31.0.0/20) is one slice of the VPC’s 172.31.0.0/16. The router applies the main route table: VPC-internal traffic matches 172.31.0.0/16 → local; everything else matches 0.0.0.0/0 → igw and exits through the Internet Gateway. Every default subnet is public for exactly this reason — the route, not a setting.

1.2.1 A Custom VPC in Practice

The default VPC is suitable for launching new instances when you are testing AWS, but creating a custom VPC allows you to:

  • Make things more secure — nothing is internet-reachable until you deliberately route it.
  • Customize your virtual network — you define your own IP address range.
  • Create subnets that are both private and public — segmenting tiers by exposure.
  • Tighten security settings — security groups, NACLs, and routing exactly as your design requires.

Walk this diagram too, because it previews half the series: the web servers (private IPs 10.0.0.5–.7) each carry an Elastic IP (198.51.100.1–.3), and their subnet’s route table includes 0.0.0.0/0 → igw — a public subnet. The database servers sit in a VPN-only subnet: no route to the Internet Gateway at all; instead, traffic to the corporate network goes to a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW), across the VPN connection, to the customer gateway on-premises. Same VPC, two completely different security postures — decided entirely by routing.

2. AWS VPC Components

Before going deep on any single piece, here is the full map. AWS networking splits naturally into two groups: the core components that live inside every VPC, and the connectivity components that link a VPC to other networks — other VPCs, AWS services, and your data center. Each component gets its own topic page in this series; this page covers the VPC itself.

2.1 Component Reference and Where Each Is Covered

Component Reference and Where Each Is Covered.
ComponentGroupOne-line purpose
SubnetsCoreSubdivisions of the VPC’s IP range, each bound to one Availability Zone — where resources launch (this page, section 5)
Route tablesCoreThe rules deciding where traffic from each subnet is directed — what makes a subnet public or private
Internet Gateway (IGW)CoreThe VPC’s door to the internet: routes traffic and performs one-to-one NAT for public IPs
NAT GatewayCoreOutbound-only internet access for private subnets — the internet can never initiate inbound
Security groups & network ACLsCoreTwo firewall layers: stateful at the instance (SG), stateless at the subnet boundary (NACL)
VPC peeringConnectivityPrivate one-to-one connection between two VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs; not transitive
AWS Transit GatewayConnectivityRegional hub-and-spoke router connecting many VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect at scale
VPC endpoints (PrivateLink)ConnectivityPrivate access to AWS services and third-party services without touching the internet — gateway endpoints (S3/DynamoDB, free) and interface endpoints (most other services)
AWS Site-to-Site VPNConnectivityEncrypted IPsec tunnels over the internet between your data center and AWS — fast to set up
AWS Direct ConnectConnectivityDedicated physical connection to AWS for consistent bandwidth and latency

How to Use This Map

Exam questions rarely test a component in isolation — they test which component solves which problem. "Private subnet must reach S3 cheaply" is the VPC endpoints row. "Block one IP address" is the NACL half of row five. "Thirty VPCs plus on-premises" is Transit Gateway. As you study each topic page, come back to this table and check you can state every row’s trigger scenario from memory.

3. How Amazon VPC Works

This section follows the structure of the official AWS documentation page "How Amazon VPC works", explaining the same seven concepts for the exam.

3.1 The VPC Resource Map

The following is a visual representation of a VPC and its resources from the Preview pane shown when you create a VPC using the AWS Management Console. For an existing VPC, you can access this visualization on the Resource map tab. This example shows the resources that are initially selected on the Create VPC page when you choose to create the VPC plus other networking resources. This VPC is configured with an IPv4 CIDR and an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR, subnets in two Availability Zones, three route tables, an internet gateway, and a gateway endpoint. Because we have selected the internet gateway, the visualization indicates that traffic from the public subnets is routed to the internet because the corresponding route table sends the traffic to the internet gateway.

3.1.1 Reading the Resource Map

  1. VPC — one VPC with the IPv4 CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 plus an Amazon-provided IPv6 block.
  2. Subnets (4) — one public and one private subnet in each of two AZs (us-east-1a and us-east-1b), each a non-overlapping /20 slice of the VPC CIDR.
  3. Route tables (3) — both public subnets share rtb-public, which sends 0.0.0.0/0 (IPv4) and ::/0 (IPv6) to the internet gateway. Each private subnet has its own route table that sends S3 traffic (a prefix list) to the gateway endpoint.
  4. Network connections (2) — the internet gateway serves exactly 2 public subnets and 0 private subnets. The S3 gateway endpoint gives the private subnets access to S3 without any internet path.

The key takeaway: the private subnets are private only because their route tables have no route to the internet gateway. Same VPC, same kind of subnet, different route table.

3.2 The Seven Concepts From the Official Docs

3.2.1 VPCs and Subnets

A VPC is a virtual network dedicated to your account, logically isolated from all others. A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside the VPC — the place resources actually launch. Subnets can be connected to the internet, to other VPCs, and to your data center, with route tables steering the traffic.

3.2.2 Default and Nondefault VPCs

The default VPC (covered in section 2) is ready on day one: default subnet per AZ, IGW attached, internet route in place, DNS hostnames on. A VPC you create yourself is a nondefault (custom) VPC — blank until you design it. Note the docs detail: if you launch an EC2 instance without specifying a subnet, AWS places it in one of the default subnets for you.

3.2.3 Route Tables

Each route is a destination (the IP range the traffic is heading to) and a target (the gateway, interface, or connection to send it through). A subnet explicitly associated with a route table uses it; otherwise it implicitly uses the main route table. See section 5, Subnets & Route Tables, for the full explanation.

3.2.4 Access the Internet

Three paths, in increasing restriction:

  • Default subnet — instances get private and public IPv4 addresses and reach the internet through the pre-wired IGW.
  • Nondefault subnet — instances get only a private IP unless you assign a public one; to give them internet access you attach an IGW and associate a public or Elastic IP.
  • NAT device — for outbound-only: NAT maps many private IPv4 addresses behind one public (Elastic) IP, letting private instances initiate connections out while unsolicited inbound connections are blocked. For IPv6, which does not use NAT, the outbound-only component is the egress-only Internet Gateway — and IPv6 routes are maintained separately from IPv4 routes.

3.2.5 Access a Corporate Or Home Network

An AWS Site-to-Site VPN makes the cloud an extension of your data center: two IPsec tunnels between a virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway on the AWS side and a customer gateway device (physical or software) on yours. The two-tunnel design is for redundancy — an exam-worthy detail.

3.2.6 Connect VPCs and Networks

VPC peering privately connects two VPCs so instances communicate as if on the same network. A Transit Gateway is the Regional virtual router interconnecting many VPCs, VPN connections, and Direct Connect gateways through one hub. Both get their own topic pages.

3.2.7 The AWS Private Global Network

A detail many candidates miss: traffic between AWS resources stays on AWS’s private global backbone — even when the destination is a public IP address of another AWS resource (with narrow exceptions such as the China Regions). Two EC2 instances in different Regions talking via public IPs are still traversing AWS’s network, not the open internet. AWS engineers the backbone to a packet-loss target of less than 0.0001% at p99 — the performance rationale behind cross-Region designs.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: “Launched an instance without choosing a subnet”→ it went to a default subnet in the default VPC

Trigger 2: “Route = destination + target”→ the anatomy of every route table entry

Trigger 3: “Outbound-only for IPv6”→ egress-only Internet Gateway (never NAT)

Trigger 4: “Site-to-Site VPN components”→ virtual private gateway (or Transit Gateway) + customer gateway, two tunnels

Trigger 5: “Does inter-Region traffic between AWS resources cross the public internet?”→ no; it rides the AWS private global backbone

4. CIDR & IP Addressing

Problem Statement

You are about to create your first production VPC and the console asks one question: the CIDR block. It feels trivial, but it is the one setting you cannot change later. It decides whether, two years from now, you can peer with a partner VPC, connect the data center, or fit the next thousand instances. Choose wrong and the fix is rebuilding the network.

On the exam, the same skill shows up as quick arithmetic: "How many addresses are in this range?", "Does this subnet fit inside this VPC?", "Do these two ranges overlap?" This section teaches you to answer all three in seconds.

4.1 What Is CIDR?

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) is the IP addressing scheme that replaced the old fixed Class A, B, and C networks. The old classes only allowed networks of three sizes (/8, /16, /24). CIDR lets a network be any size by writing an IP address together with a prefix, for example 192.168.0.0/16.

4.1.1 An IPv4 Address Is 32 Bits

Every IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as 4 octets of 8 bits each, separated by dots. Each octet ranges from 0 to 255 (8 bits give 28 = 256 values). The prefix says how many of those 32 bits are fixed:

  • The fixed bits on the left form the network address. Every address in the range shares them.
  • The remaining bits on the right are the host bits. They are free to vary, and each combination is one address in the range.

So 192.168.0.0/16 means: "keep 192.168 fixed, let everything after it vary." The range runs from 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255.

4.2 Counting Addresses: The Formula

Because each free bit doubles the number of combinations, the size of any CIDR block is:

Total addresses = 2 ^ (32 − prefix)

  • 192.168.0.0/16 → 2(32 − 16) = 216 = 65,536
  • 192.168.0.0/24 → 2(32 − 24) = 28 = 256

The Halving Rule

Every time the prefix grows by 1, the range is cut in half. /24 = 256, /25 = 128, /26 = 64, /27 = 32, /28 = 16. Every time the prefix shrinks by 1, the range doubles. /23 = 512, /22 = 1,024, /21 = 2,048, /20 = 4,096. A bigger prefix number means a smaller network, which is the most common source of confusion for beginners.

4.2.1 Picturing 65,536 Addresses

A /16 has two free octets. The third octet can take 256 values, and for each of those the fourth octet can take 256 values. That is a grid of 256 × 256 = 65,536 addresses:

4.3 Prefix Lengths and Subnet Masks

The same idea, applied to every common prefix. Reading the list top to bottom, each step frees one more bit and doubles the range:

4.3.1 The Octet Quick Memo

For the prefixes that fall exactly on an octet boundary, you can read the range without any math:

The Octet Quick Memo.
PrefixOctets that can changeSubnet mask (dotted form)Example
/32None — a single address255.255.255.255134.56.78.123/32 = just 134.56.78.123
/24Last octet255.255.255.0192.168.0.0/24 = 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.0.255
/16Last two octets255.255.0.0192.168.0.0/16 = 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255
/8Last three octets255.0.0.010.0.0.0/8 = 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255
/0All four octets0.0.0.00.0.0.0/0 = every IPv4 address

The subnet mask is just the prefix written another way: the prefix’s fixed bits are 1s, the free bits are 0s. A /24 is 24 ones followed by 8 zeros, which is 255.255.255.0. AWS uses prefix notation everywhere, but you will still see masks in older documentation and on-premises equipment.

4.3.2 Where Each Prefix Shows Up in AWS

  • /16 to /28 — the only sizes allowed for a VPC or subnet. Prefixes like /29, /30, /31, and /32 are valid CIDR, but you cannot create a VPC or subnet that small.
  • /32 — a single host. Used in security group and NACL rules, for example allowing SSH only from your office IP 203.0.113.10/32.
  • /0 — every address. 0.0.0.0/0 is the "default route" in route tables (send everything else to the IGW or NAT) and means "anywhere" in a security group rule.

4.4 Finding the Last Address of Any Range

Ranges on an octet boundary are easy. For prefixes in between, use the block size method. It takes three steps:

  1. Find the octet where the boundary falls. /17 to /24 fall in the third octet; /25 to /32 fall in the fourth.
  2. Count the free bits in that octet and compute the block size: 2 ^ (free bits in that octet).
  3. Add the block size minus 1 to that octet of the start address. Every octet to the right of it becomes 255.

Worked example: 10.0.0.0/20. The boundary is in the third octet: 20 − 16 = 4 of its 8 bits belong to the network, leaving 4 free bits. Block size = 24 = 16. So the third octet runs 0 to 15, and the fourth octet runs 0 to 255. The range is 10.0.0.0 – 10.0.15.255, which is 4,096 addresses (16 × 256). The next /20 starts at 10.0.16.0.

This is exactly how the subnets in the VPC resource map (section 3) were laid out: 10.0.0.0/20, 10.0.16.0/20, 10.0.128.0/20, 10.0.144.0/20. Each starts on a multiple of 16 in the third octet.

Exam Trap

A block must start on its boundary.

A /20 can only start where the third octet is a multiple of 16 (0, 16, 32, 48...). 10.0.8.0/20 is not a valid network start, because 8 is not a multiple of 16. Likewise, a /26 must start where the fourth octet is a multiple of 64 (0, 64, 128, 192). The console will reject a misaligned block.

4.5 Practice Exercise

Now try harder ones. Work each out on paper, then reveal the answer.

Practice Question 1. What range does 172.16.32.0/19 cover, and how many addresses is that?

Show the answer

The boundary is in the third octet, which has 3 network bits (19 − 16) and 5 free bits. Block size = 25 = 32. Range: 172.16.32.0 – 172.16.63.255. Size: 2(32−19) = 213 = 8,192 addresses.

Practice Question 2. What range does 192.168.1.64/26 cover? How many usable addresses would an AWS subnet of this size have?

Show the answer

The boundary is in the fourth octet, with 6 free bits. Block size = 26 = 64. Range: 192.168.1.64 – 192.168.1.127. That is 64 addresses, so an AWS subnet would have 64 − 5 = 59 usable.

Practice Question 3. You need a subnet for 500 instances. What is the smallest prefix that works in AWS?

Show the answer

A /24 gives 251 usable (too small). A /23 gives 512 − 5 = 507 usable, which fits. The answer is /23.

Practice Question 4. Do 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.128.0/17 overlap? Could two VPCs with these ranges be peered?

Show the answer

Yes, they overlap. 10.0.0.0/16 covers 10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255, and 10.0.128.0/17 (10.0.128.0 – 10.0.255.255) sits entirely inside it. VPC peering is not possible between overlapping CIDRs.

When in doubt, check your work with a CIDR calculator such as ipaddressguide.com/cidr, but practice until you do not need it. The exam gives you no calculator.

4.6 The Five Reserved Addresses (Memorize)

In every subnet, AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last one. For 10.0.1.0/24:

The Five Reserved Addresses (Memorize).
AddressReserved for
10.0.1.0Network address
10.0.1.1VPC router
10.0.1.2Amazon-provided DNS
10.0.1.3Reserved for future use
10.0.1.255Broadcast address (broadcast is not supported in a VPC, but the address is still reserved)
The Five Reserved Addresses (Memorize) (table 2).
Subnet prefixTotal addressesUsable in AWS
/1665,53665,531
/204,0964,091
/24256251
/266459
/28 (smallest allowed)1611

Exam Trap

Classic exam trap.

"How many usable IP addresses in a /24 subnet?" The answer is 251, never 256. The reservation applies per subnet, so it hurts small subnets most: a /28 yields just 11 usable addresses.

4.7 VPC Addressing Rules

4.7.1 IPv4 Rules

  • Size limits: a VPC CIDR must be between /16 (65,536 addresses) and /28 (16 addresses). The same limits apply to subnets.
  • Use the RFC 1918 private ranges. These are reserved for private networks and never routed on the public internet:
IPv4 Rules.
RFC 1918 rangeCoversTypical AWS VPC CIDR
10.0.0.0/810.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.25510.X.0.0/16 (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16, 10.1.0.0/16 ... 256 non-overlapping VPCs)
172.16.0.0/12172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255172.16.0.0/16 to 172.31.0.0/16 (note: the default VPC uses 172.31.0.0/16)
192.168.0.0/16192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255192.168.0.0/16 (often already used by home and office networks)
  • The primary CIDR cannot be changed after the VPC is created. If you outgrow it, you can add secondary CIDR blocks, but the original stays.
  • Never overlap with any network you might connect later: other VPCs, partner networks, or on-premises. Overlapping ranges cannot be peered or routed. A common practice is to give each VPC its own 10.X.0.0/16 from a central plan (AWS VPC IP Address Manager, IPAM, can enforce this across accounts).
  • Avoid 192.168.0.0/16 when users connect over VPN, because many home routers use that range and will collide with it.

4.7.2 IPv6 Rules

  • An Amazon-provided IPv6 block for a VPC is a /56, which holds 272 addresses (IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, and 128 − 56 = 72). Each subnet gets a /64, so one VPC can have 256 IPv6 subnets.
  • IPv6 blocks are allocated by AWS (you cannot pick the numbers) unless you bring your own range (BYOIP).
  • IPv6 addresses are globally unique and publicly routable. There is no private IPv6 range to hide behind, so "private" for IPv6 means controlling routes and using an egress-only Internet Gateway for outbound-only access.
  • A VPC always has an IPv4 CIDR. IPv6 is added alongside it (dual-stack).

4.8 Putting It Together: Carving a VPC Into Subnets

A typical plan for a 10.0.0.0/16 VPC across two AZs, using /24 subnets so the third octet tells you the tier at a glance:

Putting It Together: Carving a VPC Into Subnets.
SubnetCIDRRangeUsable
Public — AZ A10.0.1.0/2410.0.1.0 – 10.0.1.255251
Public — AZ B10.0.2.0/2410.0.2.0 – 10.0.2.255251
Private app — AZ A10.0.11.0/2410.0.11.0 – 10.0.11.255251
Private app — AZ B10.0.12.0/2410.0.12.0 – 10.0.12.255251
Private data — AZ A10.0.21.0/2410.0.21.0 – 10.0.21.255251
Private data — AZ B10.0.22.0/2410.0.22.0 – 10.0.22.255251

Six subnets use only 1,536 of the VPC’s 65,536 addresses. A /16 holds 256 such /24 subnets, so there is plenty of room to add tiers or AZs later. Leaving that headroom is the point.

5. Subnets & Route Tables

Problem Statement

Your VPC has 65,536 addresses in one big pool, but the web tier, the app tier, and the database need different exposure levels, and the whole system must survive a data center outage. One flat pool cannot express "this part faces the internet, that part never does, and everything exists in two places."

You need two things: a way to carve the pool into purposeful slices (subnets), and a way to give each slice its own rules for where traffic goes (route tables).

5.1 What a Subnet Is

  • A VPC network is partitioned into smaller networks called subnets. Each subnet is a range of IP addresses carved from the VPC CIDR, and every AWS resource launches into a specific subnet.
  • Subnets are created inside a specific Availability Zone. One subnet = one AZ. A subnet can never span AZs — one of the most-tested VPC facts.
  • You can (and should) have multiple subnets per AZ, typically one per tier: public, private app, private data.
  • Subnet CIDRs inside one VPC must not overlap each other, and each must fit inside the VPC CIDR. Sizes range from /16 to /28, the same limits as the VPC.
  • The VPC has a built-in local router that routes traffic between all its subnets. You never deploy or manage it.

5.2 Reserved Addresses and Sizing a Subnet

AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet: the first four and the last one. These cannot be assigned to an EC2 instance or any other resource. For a subnet with CIDR 10.0.0.0/24:

  • 10.0.0.0 — network address
  • 10.0.0.1 — the VPC router
  • 10.0.0.2 — mapping to the Amazon-provided DNS
  • 10.0.0.3 — reserved for future use
  • 10.0.0.255 — network broadcast address (AWS does not support broadcast in a VPC, so it is simply reserved)

5.2.1 How to Size a Subnet

Exam Tip: Always Subtract the 5 Reserved Addresses

If you need 29 IP addresses for EC2 instances:

  • You cannot choose a subnet of size /27: it has 32 addresses, and 32 − 5 = 27, which is less than 29.
  • You need a subnet of size /26: it has 64 addresses, and 64 − 5 = 59, which is more than 29.

The trap is that a /27 looks big enough until you remember the reservation.

Use this table to find the smallest subnet for any requirement:

How to Size a Subnet.
Need this many addressesSmallest subnet that fitsUsable
up to 11/2811
12 – 27/2727
28 – 59/2659
60 – 123/25123
124 – 251/24251
252 – 507/23507

Size for Growth, Not Just Today

Instances are not the only consumers of subnet addresses. Load balancer nodes, NAT Gateways, interface endpoints, Lambda ENIs, and EKS pods all take IPs from the subnet. Auto Scaling also needs room to add instances during a scale-out. In practice, leave generous headroom; a /24 or larger is common for app subnets.

5.3 Route Tables: How a Subnet Gets Its Behavior

Subnets on their own are just address ranges. What a subnet can actually reach is decided by its route table. Route tables define the routing logic for subnets.

5.3.1 What a Route Table Is

  • A route table is a set of rules called routes. Each route has a destination (the IP range the traffic is going to) and a target (where to send it: a gateway, network interface, or connection).
  • When a packet leaves a subnet, the VPC router checks that subnet’s route table and sends the packet to the matching target.
  • If several routes match, the most specific one wins (longest prefix match). A route for 10.0.5.0/24 beats a route for 0.0.0.0/0.
  • If no route matches, the packet is dropped.

5.3.2 The Local Route

Every route table automatically contains a local route for the VPC CIDR, for example 10.10.0.0/16 → local in Figure 5a. It means "traffic for any address inside the VPC stays inside the VPC," and it is why all subnets can talk to each other by default. You cannot delete the local route. To restrict subnet-to-subnet traffic, you use security groups and NACLs, not routing.

5.3.3 Main Route Table vs. Custom Route Tables

  • Every VPC has a main (default) route table, created with the VPC. By default it holds only the local route.
  • All subnets follow the main route table by default, unless you explicitly associate them with another one.
  • You can create custom (subnet-specific) route tables and associate them with particular subnets. An explicit association overrides the main table for that subnet.
  • Association rules: each subnet is associated with exactly one route table, but one route table can serve many subnets. For example, both public subnets in Figure 3a share one public route table.

Best Practice

Keep the main route table private.

Any new subnet you create silently joins the main route table. If you add an Internet Gateway route to the main table, every future subnet becomes public by accident. Leave the main table with only the local route, and create custom route tables for public and private tiers.

5.3.4 Common Route Targets

Common Route Targets.
DestinationTargetEffect on the subnet
VPC CIDR (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16)localReach every other subnet in the VPC (always present)
0.0.0.0/0Internet Gateway (igw-)Two-way internet access: the subnet becomes public
0.0.0.0/0NAT Gateway (nat-)Outbound-only internet access for a private subnet
S3 or DynamoDB prefix listGateway endpoint (vpce-)Private access to S3 or DynamoDB without the internet
Another VPC’s CIDRPeering connection (pcx-)Reach a peered VPC
On-premises CIDRVirtual private gateway (vgw-) or Transit Gateway (tgw-)Reach the corporate network over VPN or Direct Connect

Each of these targets gets its own topic page later in the series. For now, the key idea is that one route table entry changes what a whole subnet can reach.

5.4 Public vs. Private Subnets

This is one of the most heavily tested ideas on the exam, and the root of almost every VPC design decision. The first thing to know: there is no "public" or "private" checkbox on a subnet. A subnet’s type is a result of its routing, and AWS never labels it for you.

5.4.1 What Makes a Subnet Public

A public subnet is a subnet whose resources can be reached from, and can reach, the internet directly. For that to work, three things must all be true:

  1. An Internet Gateway is attached to the VPC. One IGW per VPC, attached at the VPC level.
  2. The subnet’s route table has a route to it: 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-... (and ::/0 → igw-... for IPv6). This route is what defines the subnet as public.
  3. The resource has a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP. Without one, the IGW has no public address to translate to, so the instance cannot be reached even in a public subnet.

The subnet setting "auto-assign public IPv4 address" only handles condition 3, by giving new instances a public IP at launch. It does not make a subnet public. An instance with a public IP in a subnet that has no IGW route still cannot reach the internet.

Each public subnet’s route table sends internet traffic through the Internet Gateway. EC2 instances in a public subnet can have their own public IPs or Elastic IPs (EIPs). These addresses are associated with the instance’s Elastic Network Interface (ENI), and the Internet Gateway performs the one-to-one translation (NAT) between the private and public address.

5.4.2 What Makes a Subnet Private

A private subnet is any subnet whose route table has no route to an Internet Gateway. The internet cannot start a connection to anything inside it, no matter what IP addresses or firewall rules are configured. There are two kinds:

  • Private with outbound access: the route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Instances can start connections out (patches, external APIs), but nothing can start a connection in. This is the usual home for application servers.
  • Isolated: the route table has only the local route. No internet access in either direction. This is the safest home for databases and other sensitive data.

Resources in private subnets are assigned only private IPs and cannot reach the internet directly. To reach resources or users on the internet, they go through a NAT Gateway. A NAT Gateway is a fully managed service that is highly available within one Availability Zone. To stay available across AZs, deploy at least two NAT Gateways in different AZs. If one AZ becomes unavailable, private subnets in the other AZs keep their outbound access through their own NAT Gateway.

Notice the address plan in both diagrams: the /22 VPC holds exactly 1,024 addresses, split into three /24 private subnets (768), two /26 public subnets (128), and one /25 public subnet (128). Private subnets get the larger ranges because that is where most workloads live.

What Makes a Subnet Private.
AspectPublic subnetPrivate subnet (with NAT)Isolated subnet
Default route0.0.0.0/0 → igw0.0.0.0/0 → natNone (local route only)
Inbound from internetPossible (subject to security groups and NACLs)ImpossibleImpossible
Outbound to internetYes, directlyYes, through the NAT GatewayNo
Needs public IPs?Yes, for resources that must be reachableNo — private IPs onlyNo — private IPs only
Typical residentsInternet-facing load balancers, NAT Gateways, bastion hostsApp servers, containers, VPC-attached LambdaDatabases, caches, sensitive back-end services
Security postureLowest — internet-facing, keep it minimalHigher — no inbound pathHighest — no internet path at all

5.4.3 A Simple Example

Walk the diagram:

  1. Public subnet (192.168.0.0/24, ap-south-1a) — its route table sends internet traffic to the Internet Gateway. It holds the things that must face the internet: the WordPress web server, a bastion host for admin SSH access, and the NAT Gateway.
  2. Private subnet (192.168.1.0/24, ap-south-1b) — its route table sends internet traffic to the NAT Gateway, not the IGW. The MySQL database can download patches outbound, but nothing on the internet can start a connection to it.
  3. The VPC router connects both subnets (the local route), so WordPress can reach MySQL and the bastion host can reach the database server for administration.

5.4.4 Architecture: A Three-Tier Application

A production design uses all three subnet types, mirrored in two Availability Zones. This is the reference architecture you should be able to draw from memory for the exam:

Walk the architecture from the top:

  1. Users connect over the internet to the Internet Gateway, which forwards the traffic to the Application Load Balancer. The ALB has a node in each public subnet, so it survives the loss of one AZ.
  2. The ALB forwards requests to app servers in the private app subnets. The app servers have only private IPs, so the ALB is the single front door. Nothing on the internet can reach them directly.
  3. App servers query the database in the isolated subnets over the VPC’s local route. RDS Multi-AZ keeps a standby in AZ B.
  4. App servers download patches through the NAT Gateway in their own AZ. Each private route table points at its local NAT Gateway, so an AZ failure does not cut the other AZ’s outbound access.
  5. The databases have no route out at all. Even if a database were compromised, it could not send data to the internet.

The routing for this design uses four route tables:

Architecture: A Three-Tier Application.
Route tableAssociated subnetsRoutes
rtb-publicBoth public subnets10.0.0.0/16 → local, 0.0.0.0/0 → igw
rtb-private-aPrivate app subnet, AZ A10.0.0.0/16 → local, 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-A
rtb-private-bPrivate app subnet, AZ B10.0.0.0/16 → local, 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-B
rtb-dbBoth isolated DB subnets10.0.0.0/16 → local only

Why two private route tables but only one public one? Both public subnets send traffic to the same IGW, which is Region-wide, so they can share a table. Each private subnet must point at the NAT Gateway in its own AZ, so each needs its own table.

5.4.5 How Traffic Actually Flows

Scenario 2 is the key insight. A private subnet is not protected mainly by a firewall rule that could be misconfigured. It is protected because no network path exists. Security groups and NACLs then add a second and third layer on top.

5.4.6 Reaching Private Resources When You Need To

Private does not mean unreachable for your own team. There are standard, secure ways in and out:

Reaching Private Resources When You Need To.
NeedSolutionHow it works
Serve users from private app serversInternet-facing load balancer in public subnetsThe ALB accepts public traffic and forwards it to private targets
Download patches and call external APIsNAT Gateway in a public subnetOutbound only; the internet cannot initiate connections back
Admin shell access (preferred)AWS Systems Manager Session ManagerNo inbound ports, no public IP, access controlled by IAM and logged
Admin shell access (traditional)Bastion host in a public subnetAdmins SSH to the bastion, then from it to private instances; restrict its security group to your office IP
Reach S3, DynamoDB, or other AWS services privatelyVPC endpointsTraffic stays on the AWS network, with no NAT or IGW needed

5.4.7 What Goes Where: Placement Guide

What Goes Where: Placement Guide.
ResourceSubnet typeWhy
Internet-facing ALB or NLBPublicMust accept connections from the internet
Internal load balancerPrivateOnly serves traffic from inside the VPC
NAT GatewayPublicNeeds its own route to the IGW to forward private traffic out
Bastion hostPublicMust be reachable by admins over SSH or RDP
Web and application serversPrivateReached through the load balancer, never directly
RDS, Aurora, ElastiCacheIsolated (or private)Should only ever be reached by the app tier
VPC-attached Lambda functionsPrivateUse a NAT Gateway or endpoints for outbound access (Lambda ENIs never get public IPs)

Exam Trap

Common mistakes (and exam distractors)

  • Putting the NAT Gateway in a private subnet. It then has no route to the IGW and cannot forward anything. NAT Gateways always go in public subnets.
  • An instance in a public subnet with no public IP. The route is there, but the instance still cannot be reached or reach out directly. Assign a public or Elastic IP.
  • Turning on "auto-assign public IP" to make a subnet public. That setting only hands out IPs. The IGW route is what makes the subnet public.
  • Putting the database in a public subnet "with a tight security group." One security group mistake would expose it. Databases belong in private or isolated subnets.
  • One NAT Gateway for both AZs. If its AZ fails, the other AZ loses outbound access. Use one NAT Gateway per AZ.

5.5 Why Multi-AZ Matters

  • If one AZ goes down, resources in the other AZs keep running — but only if they exist there. Design every tier across at least two AZs.
  • EC2 Auto Scaling distributes instances across the subnets (and therefore AZs) you give it. One subnet per AZ per tier is the standard pattern.
  • Mirror the layout: whatever exists in AZ-A exists identically in AZ-B. Note that Figure 5d puts each subnet in a different AZ, which is fine for a demo, but production mirrors every tier in each AZ, as in Figure 5e and the skeleton below.

Exam Trap

Scope.

VPC = Region-wide. Subnet = one AZ. An answer placing "a subnet spanning two AZs" or "a VPC spanning two Regions" is automatically wrong. High availability comes from multiple subnets in multiple AZs — never from stretching one subnet.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: “A subnet can span multiple AZs”→ false, always

Trigger 2: “Survive AZ failure”→ mirrored subnets in at least two AZs

Trigger 3: “What makes a subnet public”→ a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway in its route table, not a setting

Trigger 4: “Need 29 IPs”→ /26, not /27

Trigger 5: “Subnet not explicitly associated with a route table”→ it uses the main route table

Trigger 6: “Subnets in the same VPC can talk by default”→ yes, the local route; restrict with security groups or NACLs

Trigger 7: “Two routes match a packet”→ the most specific (longest prefix) wins

6. Internet Gateway

Problem Statement

You have built a custom VPC with a public and a private subnet, launched a web server, and given it a public IP. You open its address in a browser and nothing loads. The server cannot even download a software update. A VPC is isolated by default, and a custom VPC has no path to the internet at all until you build one.

You need a door between your VPC and the internet that is:

  • Always available, so it never becomes a single point of failure;
  • Unlimited in capacity, so it never becomes a bottleneck as traffic grows;
  • Selective, so only the subnets you choose can use it.

That door is the Internet Gateway.

6.1 What Is an Internet Gateway?

An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC component that connects your VPC to the internet. It does two jobs:

  1. It is a route table target. Subnets send internet-bound traffic to it with a route like 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-....
  2. It translates addresses (NAT) for instances with public IPv4 addresses. It maps each instance’s private IP to its public or Elastic IP, one to one.

It supports both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic. For IPv6, no translation is needed, because IPv6 addresses are already public.

6.1.1 Key Properties

Key Properties.
PropertyDetail
AttachmentOne IGW per VPC, and one VPC per IGW. A VPC that already has an IGW cannot attach a second one.
ScopeAttached at the VPC level. It does not live in a subnet or an Availability Zone, so it serves every AZ.
AvailabilityRedundant and highly available by design, with no single point of failure.
BandwidthNo bandwidth limit; it scales automatically.
CostFree. No hourly charge; you pay only for data transfer (public IPv4 addresses are billed separately).
ManagementFully managed by AWS. Nothing to size, patch, or monitor.
SecurityNo security group of its own. You control traffic with security groups and network ACLs on your resources and subnets.

6.2 How the Internet Gateway Defines Public and Private Subnets

  • The Internet Gateway connects the VPC to the internet.
  • If a subnet’s route table has a route to the internet through the Internet Gateway, it is called a public subnet.
  • If a subnet’s route table does not have a route to the internet, it is called a private subnet.
How the Internet Gateway Defines Public and Private Subnets.
Public subnet route table: destinationTarget
10.10.0.0/16Local
0.0.0.0/0Internet Gateway (igw-x)
How the Internet Gateway Defines Public and Private Subnets (table 2).
Private subnet route table: destinationTarget
10.10.0.0/16Local

The only difference between the two tables is the single 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-x route.

6.2.1 A Public IP Alone Is Not Enough

In the following diagram, the subnet in Availability Zone A is a public subnet because its route table has a route that sends all internet-bound IPv4 traffic to the Internet Gateway. Instances in the public subnet must have public IP addresses or Elastic IP addresses to communicate with the internet over the Internet Gateway.

For comparison, the subnet in Availability Zone B is a private subnet because its route table does not have a route to the Internet Gateway. Because there is no route, instances in the private subnet cannot communicate with the internet, even if they have public IP addresses.

Exam Trap

Both conditions are required.

A route without a public IP fails: the IGW has no public address to map the instance to. A public IP without a route also fails: the traffic never reaches the IGW. Exam questions often describe one half working and ask why the instance still cannot connect.

6.3 How the Internet Gateway Handles Traffic

  1. An instance in a public subnet (private IP 10.0.1.10) sends a packet to 8.8.8.8. Its route table matches 0.0.0.0/0 → igw, so the packet goes to the Internet Gateway.
  2. The IGW rewrites the source address from the private IP to the instance’s public IP (54.23.45.67) and sends the packet to the internet.
  3. The reply comes back addressed to 54.23.45.67. The IGW rewrites the destination to 10.0.1.10 and delivers it to the instance.

This is why you never see the public IP in the instance’s operating system network settings. The instance only knows its private IP; the mapping lives in the IGW. It is also why inbound connections work for public instances: the IGW knows which private IP owns each public IP.

6.4 Enabling Internet Access for a Custom VPC

The default VPC has all of this done for you. For a custom VPC, follow these steps:

  1. Create an Internet Gateway.
  2. Attach it to the VPC. It does nothing until it is attached.
  3. Add a route 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-... to the route table of each subnet that should be public. For IPv6, also add ::/0 → igw-....
  4. Give instances a public IP. Either enable "auto-assign public IPv4 address" on the subnet (applies to new instances) or associate an Elastic IP.
  5. Allow the traffic in the instance’s security group (for example, inbound HTTPS on port 443) and in the subnet’s network ACL.

To remove internet access, reverse this: delete the route to make one subnet private, or detach the IGW to cut off the whole VPC. An IGW must be detached before it can be deleted.

Troubleshooting Checklist: "My Instance Cannot Reach the Internet"

Check these in order: (1) Is an Internet Gateway attached to the VPC? (2) Does the subnet’s route table have 0.0.0.0/0 → igw? (3) Does the instance have a public or Elastic IP? (4) Do the security group and network ACL allow the traffic, including return traffic on ephemeral ports for the NACL? The first two are the most common causes.

6.5 Internet Gateway vs. NAT Gateway vs. Egress-Only Internet Gateway

Internet Gateway vs. NAT Gateway vs. Egress-Only Internet Gateway.
AspectInternet GatewayNAT GatewayEgress-only Internet Gateway
Used byPublic subnetsPrivate subnets (IPv4)Private subnets (IPv6)
DirectionInbound and outboundOutbound onlyOutbound only
Where it livesAttached to the VPCIn a public subnet, in one AZAttached to the VPC
Address translationOne-to-one (each instance’s own public IP)Many-to-one (all instances share the NAT’s Elastic IP)None (IPv6 is already public)
CostFree (data transfer only)Hourly charge + per-GB processingFree (data transfer only)
AvailabilityRedundant across the VPCRedundant within its AZ; deploy one per AZRedundant across the VPC

A NAT Gateway still depends on the Internet Gateway: it sits in a public subnet and sends its traffic out through the IGW.

7. Egress-Only Internet Gateway

Problem Statement

Your private instances have IPv6 addresses and must reach the internet over IPv6, for example to download updates and call APIs. An Internet Gateway would also let the internet connect in, and a NAT Gateway is built for IPv4.

You need an outbound-only door for IPv6: instances can start connections, but the internet cannot start one to them.

7.1 What Is an Egress-Only Internet Gateway?

  • Used for IPv6 only. It is similar to a NAT Gateway, but for IPv6.
  • Allows instances in your VPC to make outbound connections over IPv6.
  • Prevents the internet from initiating an IPv6 connection to your instances.
  • Stateful: replies to outbound requests are allowed back in.
  • No address translation: IPv6 addresses are already globally unique, so it only blocks inbound-initiated traffic.
  • Horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available. No charge for the gateway (data transfer charges still apply).
  • It has no security group of its own. Control traffic with security groups on instances and a network ACL on the subnet.

7.2 How to Use It

  • Create an egress-only Internet Gateway in the VPC.
  • In the private subnet’s route table, add ::/0 → eigw-....
  • Keep IPv4 on its own route: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway.
  • A public subnet that must also accept inbound IPv6 uses ::/0 → Internet Gateway instead.
How to Use It.
DestinationTargetPurpose
10.10.0.0/16LocalIPv4 traffic inside the VPC
2001:db8:1234:1a00::/56LocalIPv6 traffic inside the VPC
0.0.0.0/0NAT GatewayOutbound IPv4 to the internet
::/0Egress-only Internet GatewayOutbound-only IPv6 to the internet

7.3 Internet Gateway vs. NAT Gateway vs. Egress-Only Internet Gateway

Internet Gateway vs. NAT Gateway vs. Egress-Only Internet Gateway (table 2).
AspectInternet GatewayNAT GatewayEgress-only Internet Gateway
IP versionIPv4 and IPv6IPv4 (also translates IPv6-only workloads to IPv4 with NAT64)IPv6 only
DirectionTwo-wayOutbound onlyOutbound only
Typical subnetPublicPrivate (the NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet)Private
CostFreeBilled per hour and per GB processedFree (data transfer applies)

7.4 IPv6 in Your VPC: What Else Changes

  • Dual-stack mode lets you run IPv4 and IPv6 together in the same VPC and subnets, which eases migration and improves compatibility.
  • Security groups and NACLs have separate IPv4 and IPv6 rules (::/0), so you must explicitly allow or deny IPv6 traffic.
  • Route tables have separate IPv6 routes, usually ::/0 to the egress-only Internet Gateway (outbound only) or to the Internet Gateway (two-way).
  • VPC endpoints (interface and gateway) support IPv6 in many Regions, giving private IPv6 access to AWS services. Check support per service and Region.

7.5 When to Use It

  • IoT and global-scale workloads that need a very large address space.
  • Avoiding NAT bottlenecks and NAT Gateway costs for IPv6 traffic.

Mandatory Video

Exam Trap

Match the gateway to the IP version.

NAT Gateway = IPv4 outbound only. Egress-only Internet Gateway = IPv6 outbound only. An Internet Gateway is two-way, so it cannot give you outbound-only IPv6.

Trigger 3: “NAT Gateway for IPv6”→ egress-only Internet Gateway

8. Security Groups & Network ACLs

Problem Statement

Your VPC now routes traffic correctly: the load balancer is public, the app servers are private, and the database is isolated. But routing only decides where traffic can go. The security team still asks:

  • The load balancer should accept only HTTPS. How do you block every other port?
  • The database must accept connections only from the app servers, and those servers scale in and out with changing IPs. How do you write that rule?
  • A known malicious IP range is attacking you. How do you block it for every resource in a subnet at once?

AWS gives you two firewall layers to answer these: security groups at the instance level and network ACLs at the subnet level.

8.1 Two Layers of Defense

Traffic entering a subnet is checked first by the subnet’s network ACL, then by the security group attached to the resource. Both must allow it. This layered approach is called defense in depth: if one layer is misconfigured, the other still protects you.

8.2 Security Groups

8.2.1 What Is a Security Group?

  • A security group acts as a virtual firewall for EC2 instances and other resources (load balancers, RDS databases, Lambda functions in a VPC).
  • It controls inbound and outbound traffic at the instance or ENI level. It is attached to an elastic network interface (ENI), not to a subnet.
  • It is stateful: if you allow inbound traffic, the response is automatically allowed out, with no outbound rule needed. The same works in reverse.

8.2.2 Key Properties

Key Properties (table 2).
PropertyDetails
LevelInstance / ENI (elastic network interface)
RulesAllow rules only — there are no deny rules. Anything not allowed is denied.
DefaultDeny all inbound, allow all outbound
EvaluationAll rules are evaluated before a decision is made; there is no rule order
AssignmentOne instance can have multiple security groups (their rules combine)
ScopeVPC level — reusable across instances in the same VPC

8.2.3 Inbound and Outbound Rules

Each rule has three parts:

  • Protocol: TCP, UDP, ICMP, or All.
  • Port range: a single port or a range, for example 443 or 3000-3010.
  • Source (for inbound) or destination (for outbound): an IP address, a CIDR block, or another security group.

The Most Useful Feature: Referencing Another Security Group

You can use another security group as the source or destination in a rule, instead of an IP address. A rule like "allow port 3306 from the app tier’s security group" automatically covers every instance in that group, even as Auto Scaling adds and removes instances with new IPs. This is the exam’s preferred way to connect tiers.

8.2.4 Example: Securing a Three-Tier Application

Each tier gets its own security group, and each group trusts only the tier in front of it:

Example: Securing a Three-Tier Application.
Security groupInbound ruleEffect
ALB-SG (load balancer)Allow TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0Anyone on the internet can reach the ALB over HTTPS. Every other protocol and port is blocked.
APP-SG (application servers)Allow TCP 8080 from ALB-SGOnly the load balancer can reach the app servers. The internet cannot, even if it found their IPs.
DB-SG (RDS database)Allow TCP 3306 from APP-SGOnly the app servers can reach the database. Even the ALB is blocked.

No IP addresses appear anywhere after the first rule. The chain follows the traffic path: internet → ALB → app servers → database.

8.3 Network ACLs

8.3.1 What Is a Network ACL?

  • It acts as a firewall at the subnet level, checking all traffic entering and leaving the subnet.
  • It works at the subnet level, so it is automatically applied to all instances in the subnet. You do not attach it to individual instances.
  • It is stateless: inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated separately. A response is checked again on its way out, so return traffic needs its own rule.
  • Rules are evaluated in the order of rule number (1 to 32766), lowest first.

Key Takeaway

"NACLs are a great way of blocking a specific IP at the subnet level."

8.3.2 Key Properties

Key Properties (table 3).
PropertyDetails
LevelSubnet level — applies to every resource in the subnet
RulesBoth allow and deny rules
DefaultThe default NACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic. A custom NACL denies all until you add rules.
EvaluationEvaluated in number order, lowest first
First matchProcessing stops at the first matching rule
Explicit denyCan block a specific IP address or range explicitly
AssociationEach subnet has exactly one NACL; one NACL can cover many subnets

8.3.3 A Sample Rule Set

A Sample Rule Set.
Rule #TypeProtocolPortSourceAllow/Deny
100HTTPTCP800.0.0.0/0ALLOW
110HTTPSTCP4430.0.0.0/0ALLOW
120CustomTCP1024-655350.0.0.0/0ALLOW
*AllAllAll0.0.0.0/0DENY

The * rule is always last and cannot be removed: anything that no numbered rule matches is denied. Leave gaps between rule numbers (100, 110, 120) so you can insert rules later.

8.3.4 Example: The Default Network ACL

Every VPC comes with a default network ACL. It accepts everything inbound and outbound for the subnets it is associated with. Any subnet you do not explicitly associate with a custom NACL uses the default one.

Example: The Default Network ACL.
Inbound rulesRule #ProtocolPortSourceAllow/Deny
100All IPv4 trafficAll0.0.0.0/0Allow
101All IPv6 trafficAll::/0Allow
*All IPv4 trafficAll0.0.0.0/0Deny
*All IPv6 trafficAll::/0Deny
Example: The Default Network ACL (table 2).
Outbound rulesRule #ProtocolPortDestinationAllow/Deny
100All IPv4 trafficAll0.0.0.0/0Allow
101All IPv6 trafficAll::/0Allow
*All IPv4 trafficAll0.0.0.0/0Deny
*All IPv6 trafficAll::/0Deny

Read the tables using the first-match rule. Rule 100 matches every IPv4 packet and rule 101 matches every IPv6 packet, so everything is allowed. The * deny rules are never reached. (The IPv6 rules appear only if the VPC has an IPv6 CIDR block.) With the default NACL in place, all filtering is left to your security groups.

Best Practice

Do NOT modify the default NACL, create custom NACLs instead.

Every new subnet is automatically associated with the default NACL. If you add deny rules to it, you change the behavior of every subnet that uses it, including subnets created later by other teams, and troubleshooting becomes hard. Instead:

  • Create a custom NACL for each subnet tier that needs one.
  • Remember that a custom NACL denies all inbound and outbound traffic until you add rules, so add allow rules for the traffic you need, including the ephemeral port range for return traffic.
  • Explicitly associate the custom NACL with its subnets.

8.3.5 How a NACL Checks a Request and Its Response

Follow the diagram, using these rules on the private subnet’s NACL:

How a NACL Checks a Request and Its Response.
Inbound rulesOutbound rules
Rule 100: ALLOW 443Rule 100: ALLOW 443
Rule 200: ALLOW 80Rule 200: ALLOW 1024-65535
Rule *: DENY allRule *: DENY all
  1. The request comes in. A client sends a request to port 443. The NACL checks its inbound rules, matches rule 100, and allows it into the subnet.
  2. The server responds. The response goes back to the client’s ephemeral port: a random high port (1024-65535) the client picked for this connection.
  3. The response goes out. Because the NACL is stateless, it checks its outbound rules separately. Rule 200 allows 1024-65535, so the response reaches the client.

Exam Trap

The ephemeral port trap.

Without the outbound 1024-65535 rule, the request gets in but the response is blocked, and the connection looks like it hangs. This is the most common NACL mistake in real life and a favorite exam distractor. Security groups never have this problem, because they are stateful.

8.3.6 Rule Order Decides Everything

Because evaluation stops at the first match, a deny rule must have a lower number than any allow rule that matches the same traffic. To block 192.0.2.0/24 while allowing HTTPS from everyone else:

Rule Order Decides Everything.
Rule #PortSourceAllow/Deny
90All192.0.2.0/24DENY
1004430.0.0.0/0ALLOW
*All0.0.0.0/0DENY

If the deny were numbered 150 instead, rule 100 would match the attacker’s HTTPS traffic first and allow it, and the deny would never be reached.

8.4 Security Groups vs. Network ACLs

Security Groups vs. Network ACLs.
AspectSecurity groupNetwork ACL
Operates atInstance / ENI levelSubnet level
Applies toOnly resources it is attached toEvery resource in the associated subnets
StateStateful — return traffic allowed automaticallyStateless — return traffic needs its own rule
Rule typesAllow onlyAllow and deny
EvaluationAll rules, then decideNumber order; first match wins
Default (inbound)Deny allDefault NACL: allow all. Custom NACL: deny all.
Default (outbound)Allow allDefault NACL: allow all. Custom NACL: deny all.
Block a specific IPNot possibleYes, with a deny rule
Reference another SGYesNo — CIDR ranges only
Ephemeral portsNo rule neededMust be allowed for return traffic

8.4.1 When to Use Each

When to Use Each.
RequirementUseWhy
Allow specific ports to an EC2 instanceSecurity groupFine-grained control at the instance level
Block a specific IP address from a subnetNetwork ACLOnly NACLs can deny
Block a whole CIDR range from every resource in a subnetNetwork ACLSubnet-wide deny
Allow the app server to talk only to the databaseSecurity groupSecurity group rules can reference other security groups

8.5 Exam-Style Question

Exam-Style Question 1

A solutions architect is designing a three-tier web application on AWS. The architecture consists of an Application Load Balancer in the web tier, EC2 instances running the application logic in the app tier, and an Amazon RDS database in the database tier. The security team has the following requirements:

  1. The Application Load Balancer must be accessible from the internet on ports 80 and 443.
  2. The EC2 application servers must only accept traffic from the Application Load Balancer, not directly from the internet.
  3. The RDS database must only accept connections from the EC2 application servers.
  4. A known malicious IP address block 192.0.2.0/24 must be completely blocked from reaching ANY resource in the VPC.
  5. The EC2 application servers need to download software patches from the internet but must NOT be directly reachable from the internet.

Which combination of configurations satisfies ALL five requirements? (Select TWO)

  1. Place the ALB in a public subnet with a route to the Internet Gateway. Place EC2 instances and RDS in private subnets with no route to the Internet Gateway. Attach a security group to the EC2 instances that allows inbound traffic only from the ALB’s security group on the application port. Attach a security group to RDS that allows inbound traffic only from the EC2 security group on port 3306.
  2. Place all resources (ALB, EC2, and RDS) in public subnets so they can communicate freely. Use security groups on each resource to restrict traffic between tiers. Add a deny rule to the EC2 security group to block 192.0.2.0/24.
  3. Add a network ACL DENY rule with a low rule number to block inbound traffic from 192.0.2.0/24 on ALL ports on the subnets containing the ALB, EC2 instances, and RDS database.
  4. Configure a security group deny rule on the ALB security group to block all traffic from 192.0.2.0/24 before it enters the VPC.
  5. Place the EC2 instances in a private subnet with a route to a NAT Gateway in the public subnet for outbound internet access. Ensure the EC2 instances have no Elastic IP addresses and no direct route to the Internet Gateway.

(Source: CloudExpert Solutions SAA-C03 course.) Work it out before opening the analysis.

Show the analysis

Best answer: A and C.

A covers requirements 1, 2, and 3: the ALB is public, the app servers and database are private, and the security group chain (ALB-SG → APP-SG → DB-SG) lets each tier accept traffic only from the tier in front of it. It also covers the "not directly reachable" half of requirement 5.

C covers requirement 4. Only a network ACL can deny traffic, and a low rule number makes the deny match before any allow rule. Applying it to every subnet blocks the range from every resource.

B is wrong twice: it puts the database in a public subnet, and security groups cannot have deny rules. D is wrong for the same reason: security groups have no deny rules, and they do not act "before traffic enters the VPC."

A note on E: E is a correct configuration, and it is the only option that gives the app servers outbound access for patches. Strictly, no two options satisfy all five requirements: A and C leave the patch requirement unmet, so a complete design needs A, C, and E. On the real exam, questions are reviewed so that the stated number of answers is enough. If you see a question like this, choose the options that cover the most requirements and cannot be replaced by any other option, here A and C.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: “Block a specific IP or CIDR range”→ network ACL deny rule

Trigger 2: “Allow the database to accept traffic only from the app tier”→ security group referencing the app tier’s security group

Trigger 3: “Return traffic is automatically allowed”→ security group (stateful)

Trigger 4: “Rules evaluated in number order”→ network ACL

Trigger 5: “Request gets in but the response never returns”→ NACL missing the ephemeral port range

Trigger 6: “Security group deny rule”→ does not exist; that option is always wrong

Trigger 7: “Default NACL behavior”→ allows all inbound and outbound traffic

Trigger 8: “Custom NACL behavior”→ denies all until you add rules

9. Hands-On Demo: Create a VPC

Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) enables you to launch AWS resources into a virtual network that you have defined. This virtual network closely resembles a traditional network that you’d operate in your own data center, with the benefits of using the scalable infrastructure of AWS.

9.1 What You Will Build

What You Will Build.
SettingValue
NameVPC A
IPv4 CIDR block10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses)
IPv6Not enabled
TenancyDefault
DNS hostnamesEnabled (after creation)

9.2 Step 1: Open the VPC Console

Navigate to the Your VPCs tab in the VPC section of the console and click the Create VPC button.

9.3 Step 2: Configure the VPC Settings

Fill in the form as follows, then click Create VPC:

  • Select VPC only under Resources to create.
  • Enter VPC A as the Name tag.
  • Specify 10.0.0.0/16 as the IPv4 CIDR block.
  • Do not enable IPv6.
  • Leave Default selected as Tenancy.
  • Accept the proposed Tags.
  • Click Create VPC.

9.3.1 What Each Setting Means

What Each Setting Means.
SettingOptionsWhat to know
Resources to createVPC only / VPC and more"VPC only" creates just the VPC, so you build each component yourself. "VPC and more" also creates subnets, route tables, an Internet Gateway, and optional NAT Gateways and endpoints in one go, which is the resource map you saw in section 3.
Name tagAny textCreates a tag with the key Name. Tags help you find resources and track costs.
IPv4 CIDR blockManual input / IPAM-allocatedA /16 to /28 range, ideally from RFC 1918 (section 4). IPAM can allocate non-overlapping ranges from a central plan. The primary CIDR cannot be changed later.
IPv6 CIDR blockNone / IPAM-allocated / Amazon-provided / owned by meOptional. An Amazon-provided block is a /56. You can add one later.
TenancyDefault / DedicatedDefault runs instances on shared hardware. Dedicated forces every instance onto single-tenant hardware, which costs much more. Use Default unless a compliance rule requires otherwise.

9.4 Step 3: Review the New VPC

After completing these steps, you should have a new VPC listed under Your VPCs.

9.4.1 Reading the Details Page

Creating "only" a VPC actually created several things. Each field connects to a concept from this lesson:

Reading the Details Page.
FieldValueWhat it tells you
StateAvailableThe VPC is ready to use.
IPv4 CIDR10.0.0.0/16The address pool your subnets will be carved from.
Default VPCNoThis is a custom VPC, so nothing is pre-wired: no subnets, no Internet Gateway.
Main route tablertb-...Created automatically with only the local route (section 5).
Main network ACLacl-...The default NACL, which allows all traffic (section 8).
DHCP options setdopt-...Tells instances which DNS servers and domain name to use. The default points at the Amazon resolver.
DNS resolutionEnabledInstances can use the Amazon-provided DNS resolver.
DNS hostnamesDisabledInstances will not get public DNS names. Custom VPCs start with this off, which is why the next step enables it.

AWS also creates a default security group for the VPC. It is not shown on this page, but you will find it under Security groups.

9.5 Step 4: Edit the VPC Settings

Click Actions and select Edit VPC settings from the dropdown.

The same menu also has Edit CIDRs, where you can add a secondary CIDR block, and Create flow log, which records traffic metadata for the VPC.

9.6 Step 5: Enable DNS Hostnames

Check the box to enable DNS hostnames and select Save.

With both DNS resolution and DNS hostnames enabled, instances with public IPs get public DNS names, and features such as Route 53 private hosted zones and private DNS for VPC interface endpoints work correctly.

Congratulations, your first VPC is now built.

What Is Still Missing

VPC A exists, but you cannot usefully launch anything into it yet. It has no subnets, no Internet Gateway, and only the main route table. The next steps are the ones you studied in sections 5 to 7: create subnets in two Availability Zones, attach an Internet Gateway, add route tables, and set up security groups and NACLs. GLAB 269.1 in section 6 walks through all of them.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: “Instances in a new custom VPC do not get public DNS names”→ DNS hostnames is disabled by default; enable it

Trigger 2: “Private hosted zone or interface endpoint DNS not resolving”→ check that both DNS resolution and DNS hostnames are enabled

Trigger 3: “Ran out of addresses in the VPC”→ add a secondary CIDR with Edit CIDRs

Trigger 4: “All instances must run on single-tenant hardware”→ Dedicated tenancy
